segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason, since we have this service, just as we were shown mercy, we do not lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rather, we have renounced the shameful things that are kept hidden. We do not walk in cunning or tamper with the word of God, but by making the truth visible we commend ourselves to every person’s conscience in the sight of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And even if our good news is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In their case the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelieving, so that they do not see the light of the good news of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the God who said,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Light will shine out of darkness,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: is the one who has shone in our hearts to bring the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the surpassing power may be God’s and not from us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are afflicted in every way but not crushed, at a loss but not utterly at a loss,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: persecuted but not abandoned, struck down but not destroyed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always carrying around in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we who are alive are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be made visible in our mortal flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So death is at work in us, but life in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But having the same spirit of faith, in keeping with what is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I believed, therefore I spoke,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: we too believe, and therefore we also speak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that the one who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and will present us together with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all of this is for your sake, so that grace, increasing through an increasing number of people, may make thanksgiving overflow to the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore we do not lose heart. Even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our light, momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that surpasses all measure,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as we fix our gaze not on what is seen but on what is not seen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is not seen is eternal.

notes.note: The Greek word was an everyday term for service or for carrying out a task on someone’s behalf, and did not name a religious office. Most English versions use “ministry” here. That word now suggests a clergy profession, and it hides the link with the related words for “servant” and “serve”.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it is now heard as a religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, here the present age as opposed to the age to come. Many versions keep “world”, though several recent ones have “age”. Most interpreters take the phrase to refer to Satan. A minority, including some ancient commentators, took it to mean God himself.

notes.phrase: so that they do not see
notes.note: The verb can mean “see clearly” or “shine”. On the second reading the clause would be “so that the light of the good news … does not shine on them”. Most modern translations and lexicons prefer “see” here, but the matter is not settled.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by another. It is not the word for a hired servant. Many English versions soften it to “servants”. The stronger word sharpens Paul’s contrast between proclaiming Jesus as Lord and presenting himself as belonging to the Corinthians.

notes.phrase: Light will shine out of darkness
notes.note: This is not an exact quotation of any one passage. It recalls God’s first words in creation, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and perhaps also Isaiah 9:2, where light shines on people in darkness. Paul presents the coming of the knowledge of Christ as an act of the same creator.

notes.phrase: at a loss but not utterly at a loss
notes.note: The Greek pairs a verb with its own intensified form, a wordplay the traditional rendering loses. The first verb means to be at a loss or without resources. The second adds a prefix meaning “completely”.

Paul does not use the ordinary word for death here, which appears in the next two verses. This rarer noun can mean either the process of being put to death or the resulting state of deadness. “Dying” takes it as the process, which fits the ongoing dangers just listed. Many versions simply have “death”.

This is the ordinary Greek verb for handing a person into someone else’s power. It is the same verb used throughout the Gospels for Jesus being handed over to the authorities and to death. Rendering it the same way here lets the reader hear that echo.

“Spirit” may mean a disposition, the same believing attitude as the psalmist’s. It may instead mean the Holy Spirit as the one who produces faith, which would be written “Spirit”. Most translations use the lowercase reading, but a number of scholars defend the reference to God’s Spirit.

The quotation is from Psalm 116:10 in the wording of the ancient Greek translation, where it is numbered Psalm 115:1. The psalm is a thanksgiving by someone rescued from death, which suits Paul’s argument here. The Hebrew of the line is harder and is translated in various ways.

notes.phrase: increasing through an increasing number of people
notes.note: The Greek plays on two related words for “more”, and its syntax can be divided in more than one way. “Through the greater number” may go with the grace that increases, as here. It may instead go with the thanksgiving, giving “grace, having increased, may cause thanksgiving to overflow through the many”. The overall sense is the same: more people receiving grace means more thanks to God.

Paul sets the “light” affliction against a “weight” of glory. In Hebrew the usual word for glory is related to the word for heaviness, and Paul may be playing on that association. “Eternal” here means belonging to the age to come, in contrast with “this age” in verse 4, as well as unending.

candidates.reason: Versions split between “slave” and “servant” across the Gospels, Paul’s self-descriptions and the household codes, and readers would be misled by seeing it vary.
The figurative sense (conduct one’s life) recurs throughout Paul and John and is rendered variously “walk”, “live”, “behave”; one decision is needed on whether to keep the Semitic idiom.
“Preach” versus “proclaim” varies across versions and books; the word means a herald’s public announcement and should be uniform.
Rendered “flesh”, “body”, “human nature” or “sinful nature” across versions; the neutral sense here and the loaded Pauline sense elsewhere need a coordinated policy.

The verb covers “perish”, “destroy”, “lose” and “be lost” across the Gospels and letters, and the participle “those who are perishing” is a recurring Pauline category that should read the same everywhere.
